content: A blood-borne disease refers to any disease that can be transmitted through the contamination of blood. Common examples include HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and viral hemorrhagic fevers. Diseases that are not primarily transmitted through direct blood contact, but rather through insects or other vectors, are more accurately categorized as vector-borne diseases, even though the infectious agent may still be present in the blood. Examples of vector-borne diseases include West Nile virus and malaria. Many blood-borne diseases can also be spread through other routes of transmission. Because it is often impossible to determine the specific pathogens present in any given sample of blood, and because some blood-borne diseases can be fatal, standard medical protocols treat all blood and bodily fluids as potentially infectious. Blood intended for transfusion undergoes rigorous screening to detect and exclude many blood-borne pathogens. Additionally, needle exchange programs aim to decrease the transmission of blood-borne diseases among individuals who use intravenous drugs.
